title: How to Find Hidden Cameras in a Changing Room or Bathroom
excerpt: Check any changing room or bathroom for hidden cameras: where lenses hide, mirror and flashlight tests, plus exactly what to do if you find one.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
If you are standing in a changing room or a public bathroom wondering whether a camera is watching, do this first: keep your clothes on and give the room a two-minute sweep before you undress. Small tiled rooms give a hidden lens very few places to sit with a clear view of the whole space, which is exactly why a slow, methodical check works better than any gadget.

Here is that check in order, using nothing but your phone and your eyes: likely hiding spots, a mirror test, a flashlight sweep, the limits of detectors, and what to do if you find something.

Pause at the door and read the room

Stand just inside the door and read the layout before touching anything. A camera needs a view of where people undress, which in a cubicle means one of three sightlines: facing the bench from the opposite wall, looking down from a high corner or vent, or looking sideways through a partition at about chest height. Spot which ones exist, and you know where to look.

Stay dressed while you check, keep your belongings with you, and if anything feels wrong before you even start, switch cubicles and mention it to staff on your way out.

Where a lens actually hides in a small tiled room

Work top to bottom in a slow circle. Start high: smoke detectors, vents, sprinkler housings, lifted ceiling tiles, and partition tops. A real smoke detector faces straight down with no lens; anything with an off-center dark dot, a mismatched hole, or a device angled at the bench deserves a closer look.

Move to eye level: hooks, clocks, air fresheners, stray USB chargers, and dispensers with an odd extra hole. Ask of each one whether it needs power or a hole to do its job; a coat hook has no reason to have a pinhole, a glow, or a wire out of its back. Finish low: under-bench gaps, trash cans facing the bench, and bags left behind by previous occupants.

The hiding spots people miss behind partitions

Check the partition itself: fresh-looking holes at torso height, newer screws, or tape covering one suspicious spot. Sight along the wall at an angle instead of head-on; a drilled hole catches the light differently.

The fingertip test for two-way mirrors, and what it really proves

Test any full-size mirror with your fingertip pressed flat to the glass. On an ordinary mirror a visible gap sits between your finger and its reflection, caused by the glass thickness over the backing. If finger and reflection appear to touch with almost no gap, the mirror needs a closer look.

Treat this as a screen, not a verdict, since lighting and acrylic can blur the result. Back it up two ways: cup your hands around your eyes and lean in to see whether light or space sits behind the glass, and tap the surface. A backed mirror sounds dull and solid; an open-backed panel sounds hollow. Report a mirror that fails both checks; never try to remove it.

How to sweep with your phone flashlight

Dim the room lights if you can, hold your phone flashlight near your eye line, and scan slowly. Watch for a tiny sharp glint, often blue-green or white, that stays fixed while surrounding surfaces shift. That pinprick is a lens coating bouncing light straight back.

What a real lens glint looks like

Ordinary shine washes broadly across plastic; a lens glint is a hard pinprick that vanishes when you shift sideways. Scan vents slat by slat, photograph anything that glints, and never poke tools into a suspect hole.

When a detector helps and when it misleads

Handheld radio-frequency detectors listen for wireless signals some cameras transmit. If you carry one, switch off your own hotspot and Bluetooth first, then sweep slowly; a steady alert near one object deserves attention. But limits matter: many cameras record to a memory card and transmit nothing, so silence proves nothing, and in a mall full of routers, stray beeps prove little.

Red-filtered lens-finder viewers are more useful in small rooms, since they make reflections pop whether or not the camera transmits. Either way, detectors supplement the visual sweep; they never overrule what your eyes can see.

What to do if you find something

Stop, get dressed, and do not touch the device; handling it can destroy fingerprints and let whoever placed it claim you planted it. Photograph it in place plus the wider room, and note the shop name, cubicle number, and time.

Brief staff, step out, and call the police non-emergency line, or emergency services if someone detains you or tampers with the device. Hold photos off social media until officers advise you. Laws on recording in private spaces vary by state and country, so report facts and let local authorities apply the law in your jurisdiction.

One last habit: repeat this two-minute sweep every time you undress outside your own home, and never accuse staff or fellow customers over a network-scanner app, since most flagged devices are just routers and smart TVs.
